did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 120 opens with the heading “A Song of Ascents,” and the psalmist describes calling to the Lord from distress and receiving His answer.
Did you know? The phrase “In my distress” presents the trouble as a personal, direct experience in the first person: the psalmist himself cries out to the Lord.

Did you know? The request “Deliver my soul” does not refer here to an explicitly described physical danger, but to deliverance from “lying lips” and “a deceitful tongue”—harm caused by misleading speech.
Did you know? The question “What will He give you, and what more will He add to you?” is rhetorical, casting doubt on the benefit of deceitful speech and what it adds for the person who uses it.

Did you know? The deceitful tongue is described through vivid images of “the sharp arrows of a warrior” and “glowing coals of broomwood,” presenting speech as harmful and capable of causing severe consequences.
Did you know? The psalmist mentions “Meshech” and “the tents of Kedar” as he describes feeling that he lives among places or groups he regards as foreign and opposed to him.
Did you know? The repetition of verbs related to dwelling—“I have dwelt,” “I have lived,” and “she dwells”—emphasizes that living alongside those who hate peace is prolonged, not momentary.

Did you know? The final verse sets up a clear contrast: “I am for peace,” while “they are for war.” The psalmist declares his desire for peace, even though his words are answered with an intention to wage war.
